newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thai markets gain after weeks of decline.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thai markets gain after weeks of decline.

text.p: After weeks of declines, the Thai stock market ended higher on Monday as investors reacted favourably to a multi-billion dollar market support fund and an end to negative news for the time being, brokers said.

The key index finished 2.84 percent higher, gaining 15.91 points to close at 577.10. Turnover was busy ahead of a religious holiday on Tuesday with about 4.1 billion baht ($157.7 million) of shares changing hands.
Brokers said the market was helped by the new 50-billion baht ($1.92-billion) market support fund, announced at the weekend by the finance minister, and positive export figures.
"I think the market support fund helped boost market sentiment. Comments by the central bank governor on improved March exports also lifted the market," said Samart Rusmeerojwong of James Capel Asia.
Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said on Saturday that Thai commercial banks volunteered to pool the 50-billion-baht fund to help shore up the market, which tumbled to near eight-year lows last week.

Brokers said comments by Bank of Thailand Governor Rerngchai Marakanond shortly before the market closed added more positive sentiment to investors, who have seen the bourse plunge 15 percent in the first half of May.
Rerngchai said Thai exports rose 4.8 percent year-on-year in March and averaged 4.4 percent growth during the first four months of the year.
He said his preliminary export figures were based on foreign exchange transactions that local exporters and importers conducted through the central bank.

In a separate statement, made after the market closed, the Commerce Ministry said first quarter exports rose 3.0 percent over the same period last year to total 365.42 billion baht. It said exports grew eight percent the same period last year.

Analysts said the positive reaction to the figures -- which although positive were not so high -- was a sign that the market was just seeking anything that was not bad news. They said the fundamental economic problems that had brought the bourse down recently had still not yet been solved.
"Let's hope it continues," said one foreign analyst. "But it could be just a flash in the pan.
Concern over Thailand's sluggish export performance and ailing property sector have been dogging the bourse and foreign exchange markets in the past few months.

Exports contracted by 0.2 percent in 1996 after growing by more than 20 percent in 1995. The sluggish export performance contributed to the country's gross domestic product growth slowing to 6.7 percent -- the slowest level in a decade.
The Thai currency, which came under a fierce attack last week as investors aggressively sold baht for dollars, ended firmer against the dollar as many foreign players unwound long dollar positions.
The baht was quoted at 25.650/25.750 bid/ask to the dollar late, against 25.810/25.850 in morning trade.
Dealers said the Bank of Thailand still maintained its request for Thai banks not to sell baht to offshore parties in order to block speculation.

The central bank on Friday made it clear that foreign speculators who earlier sold the baht heavily for dollars would have to pay a high price when they bought back firmer baht to square their positions.
Rerngchai also said on Monday that Thailand would not resort to additional budget cuts to help balance its 1996/1997 budget, but will raise some taxes to offset falling tax revenue.
The governor's statement was in line with earlier remarks by Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, who said further budget cuts would aggravate the bearish Thai economy.
